proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(\mathbf P=(P_n)\in
\mathcal B_{\epsilon,M,c_0,v_0,v_1}\), and suppress the row subscript on
\(p_k,\pi_k,\mu_{ak}\).  All constants below may depend on
\(\epsilon,c_0,K_0\), but not on \(n,d_n\), or the chosen member of the
triangular class.  Membership in \(def:balanced\text{-}local\text{-}class\)
gives, separately, iid sampling, fixed overlap, the cell-mean envelope, the
conditional fourth-central-moment envelope, the lower cell-mass bound,
\(d_n=o(\sqrt n)\), and
\[
 v_0M^2\le V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n)\le v_1M^2.
\tag{1}
\]

First derive the nuisance rates rather than assuming them.  For a validation
fold \(I_s\), write \(m_s=n-|I_s|\) for its training size.  Since \(K_0\) is
fixed and the fold sizes differ by at most one, \(m_s\ge c_Kn\) for a constant
\(c_K>0\).  Let \(N_{ak,-s}\) and \(N_{k,-s}\) be the corresponding training
arm-cell and cell counts.  Cauchy--Schwarz and
\(ass:conditional\text{-}fourth\text{-}moment\) give
\[
 E_{P_n}[(Y-\mu_{ak})^2\mid X=k,A=a]
 \le
 \{E_{P_n}[(Y-\mu_{ak})^4\mid X=k,A=a]\}^{1/2}
 \le M^2.
\tag{2}
\]
If \(N\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,q)\), direct integration of the binomial
probability generating function gives
\[
 E[(N+1)^{-1}]=\frac{1-(1-q)^{m+1}}{(m+1)q},
 \qquad
 N^{-1}\mathbf1\{N>0\}\le2(N+1)^{-1}.
\tag{3}
\]
Conditionally on \(N_{ak,-s}=r>0\), the fitted cell mean is the average of
\(r\) observations from the conditional arm-cell law.  By (2), its conditional
mean-squared error is at most \(M^2/r\).  When \(r=0\), the zero fallback in
\(def:saturated\text{-}one\text{-}step\) has squared error at most \(M^2\) by
\(ass:cell\text{-}mean\text{-}envelope\).  With
\(q_{ak}=P_n(X=k,A=a)\ge\epsilon p_k\), equations (2)--(3) therefore imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 E\!\left[\sum_{k=1}^{d_n}p_k
  (\widehat\mu_{ak}^{(-s)}-\mu_{ak})^2\right]
 &\le M^2\sum_{k=1}^{d_n}p_k
 \left\{e^{-m_sq_{ak}}+\frac{2}{(m_s+1)q_{ak}}\right\}\\
 &\le C_\epsilon M^2
 \left\{e^{-c_\epsilon m_s/d_n}+\frac{d_n}{m_s}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]
The last inequality uses \(p_k\ge c_0/d_n\) and
\(\sum_kp_k=1\).  For the propensity estimate, condition on
\(N_{k,-s}\).  On a nonempty cell its unprojected empirical proportion has
conditional variance at most \(1/(4N_{k,-s})\); on an empty cell its squared
error is at most one.  Projection on
\([\epsilon/2,1-\epsilon/2]\) cannot increase distance from
\(\pi_k\in[\epsilon,1-\epsilon]\).  Repeating (3) gives
\[
 E\!\left[\sum_{k=1}^{d_n}p_k
  (\widehat\pi_k^{(-s)}-\pi_k)^2\right]
 \le C\left\{e^{-c m_s/d_n}+\frac{d_n}{m_s}\right\}.
\tag{5}
\]
Because \(n/d_n\to\infty\), the exponential terms are smaller than any
inverse power of \(n\).  Markov's inequality applied to (4)--(5), for each of
the fixed number of folds, yields
\[
 \|\widehat\mu_a^{(-s)}-\mu_a\|_{P_n,2}
   =O_{Q_{P_n}^{(n)}}(M\sqrt{d_n/n}),
 \qquad
 \|\widehat\pi^{(-s)}-\pi\|_{P_n,2}
   =O_{Q_{P_n}^{(n)}}(\sqrt{d_n/n}).
\tag{6}
\]

Define the uncentered augmented score
\[
 g(O;\eta)=m_1(X)-m_0(X)
 +\frac{A\{Y-m_1(X)\}}{e(X)}
 -\frac{(1-A)\{Y-m_0(X)\}}{1-e(X)},
\tag{7}
\]
where \(\eta=(e,m_0,m_1)\), and let
\(\eta_0=(\pi,\mu_0,\mu_1)\).  The definitions of the conditional means,
fixed overlap, and \(def:ate\text{-}functional\) give
\[
 E_{P_n}[g(O;\eta_0)]=\tau(P_n),
 \qquad g(O;\eta_0)-\tau(P_n)=\phi_{P_n}(O).
\tag{8}
\]
For the nuisance estimate trained outside fold \(s\), put
\(D_s(O)=g(O;\widehat\eta^{(-s)})-g(O;\eta_0)\).  Conditioning on the
training sample and evaluating (7) within each cell gives the exact
orthogonality remainder
\[
 P_nD_s=\sum_{k=1}^{d_n}p_k
 (\widehat\pi_k^{(-s)}-\pi_k)
 \left\{
 \frac{\widehat\mu_{1k}^{(-s)}-\mu_{1k}}
      {\widehat\pi_k^{(-s)}}
 +\frac{\widehat\mu_{0k}^{(-s)}-\mu_{0k}}
      {1-\widehat\pi_k^{(-s)}}
 \right\}.
\tag{9}
\]
Every denominator in (9) is at least \(\epsilon/2\).  Cauchy--Schwarz and
(6) therefore show
\[
 |P_nD_s|=O_{Q_{P_n}^{(n)}}(Md_n/n)
          =o_{Q_{P_n}^{(n)}}(Mn^{-1/2}),
\tag{10}
\]
where the last equality uses \(ass:local\text{-}dimension\).

The same score algebra, \(|\widehat\pi-\pi|\le1\), the clipped denominators,
and (2) imply the conditional second-moment bound
\[
 P_nD_s^2\le C_\epsilon\left[
 \sum_{a=0}^1\sum_{k=1}^{d_n}p_k
 (\widehat\mu_{ak}^{(-s)}-\mu_{ak})^2
 +M^2\sum_{k=1}^{d_n}p_k
 (\widehat\pi_k^{(-s)}-\pi_k)^2\right]
 =O_{Q_{P_n}^{(n)}}(M^2d_n/n).
\tag{11}
\]
Conditionally on the training data, observations in \(I_s\) are independent
of \(\widehat\eta^{(-s)}\).  Hence
\[
 (\mathbb P_{I_s}-P_n)D_s
 =O_{Q_{P_n}^{(n)}}(M\sqrt{d_n}/n).
\tag{12}
\]
Summing (9)--(12) over the fixed number of folds, with weights
\(|I_s|/n\), and using the definition of \(\widehat\tau^{\mathrm{OS}}\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \widehat\tau^{\mathrm{OS}}-\tau(P_n)
 &=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\{g(O_i;\eta_0)-\tau(P_n)\}
   +O_P(Md_n/n)+O_P(M\sqrt{d_n}/n)\\
 &=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_{P_n}(O_i)
   +o_P(n^{-1/2}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]
Here and below the final little-oh is under \(Q_{P_n}^{(n)}\); \(M\) is the
fixed scale indexing the class.

It remains to verify the variance statement.  From
\(|\mu_{ak}|\le M\), \(|\tau(P_n)|\le2M\), fixed overlap, and
\(ass:conditional\text{-}fourth\text{-}moment\), the inequality
\(|x_1+x_2+x_3|^4\le27\sum_{j=1}^3|x_j|^4\) applied to
\(def:efficient\text{-}influence\text{-}function\) yields
\[
 E_{P_n}|\phi_{P_n}(O)|^4\le C_\epsilon M^4.
\tag{14}
\]
Consequently Chebyshev's inequality, (1), and (14) give
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_{P_n}(O_i)^2
   -V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n)=o_P(M^2),
 \qquad
 \overline\phi_n^2=o_P(M^2).
\tag{15}
\]
Furthermore, conditioning fold by fold in (11) and applying Markov's
inequality gives
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{s=0}^{K_0-1}\sum_{i\in I_s}D_s(O_i)^2
 =O_P(M^2d_n/n)=o_P(M^2).
\tag{16}
\]
Writing the fitted score as
\(\widehat\psi_i=\tau(P_n)+\phi_{P_n}(O_i)+D_s(O_i)\) for
\(i\in I_s\), the elementary inequality
\[
 \left|\frac1n\sum_i(u_i+v_i-\overline u-\overline v)^2
       -\frac1n\sum_i(u_i-\overline u)^2\right|
 \le2\left\{\frac1n\sum_i(u_i-\overline u)^2
             \frac1n\sum_i(v_i-\overline v)^2\right\}^{1/2}
      +\frac1n\sum_i(v_i-\overline v)^2
\tag{17}
\]
with \(u_i=\phi_{P_n}(O_i)\), \(v_i=D_s(O_i)\), together with
(15)--(16), proves
\[
 \widehat V^{\mathrm{OS}}-V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n)=o_P(M^2).
\tag{18}
\]
Division in (18) is legitimate by the lower bound in (1), and proves
\(\widehat V^{\mathrm{OS}}/V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n)\to1\).

Finally, (1) and (14) imply
\[
 \sup_n\frac{E_{P_n}|\phi_{P_n}(O)|^4}
                 {V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n)^2}
 \le C_\epsilon/v_0^2<\infty.
\tag{19}
\]
The mean-zero identity required by
\(lem:order\text{-}one\text{-}self\text{-}normalized\text{-}clt\) is (8),
and iid sampling and positive variance are supplied by
\(ass:iid\text{-}sampling\) and (1).  That cited order-one result and (19)
therefore give
\[
 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_{P_n}(O_i)}
 {\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n[\phi_{P_n}(O_i)-\overline\phi_n]^2\right\}^{1/2}}
 \Rightarrow N(0,1).
\tag{20}
\]
By (15), the denominator in (20), divided by
\(\sqrt{nV_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n)}\), converges in probability to one.  For any
\(x\in\mathbb R\) and \(0<\delta<1\), intersecting with the event that this
ratio lies in \([1-\delta,1+\delta]\) sandwiches the distribution function of
the oracle standardized mean between the distribution functions in (20) at
the smaller and larger of \(x/(1-\delta)\) and \(x/(1+\delta)\), up to a
probability tending to zero.
First let \(n\to\infty\) and then \(\delta\downarrow0\); continuity of the
standard-normal distribution function proves
\[
 \frac{1}{\sqrt{nV_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n)}}
 \sum_{i=1}^n\phi_{P_n}(O_i)\Rightarrow N(0,1).
\tag{21}
\]
Combining (13), (21), and the lower variance bound in (1) proves the final
displayed normal limit and completes the proof of the narrowed theorem.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(\mathbf P=(P_n)\) be a triangular sequence for which, in row \(n\),
\(O_1,\ldots,O_n\) are independent with common law \((P_n)_O\).  If
\(E_{P_n}[\phi_{P_n}(O)]=0\),
\(0<V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n)=E_{P_n}[\phi_{P_n}(O)^2]\), and
\[
 \sup_n\frac{E_{P_n}[|\phi_{P_n}(O)|^4]}
                 {V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n)^2}<\infty,
\]
then
\[
 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_{P_n}(O_i)}
 {\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n
 [\phi_{P_n}(O_i)-n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n\phi_{P_n}(O_j)]^2\right\}^{1/2}}
 \Rightarrow N(0,1).
\]

open_obligations.obstruction: The stipulated transform \(\psi(x)=\tfrac12\log\{(1+x+x^2/2)/(1-x+x^2/2)\}\) satisfies \(\psi'(x)=2(2-x^2)/(x^4+4)\), so it is not globally monotone. For odd \(B\ge3\), block values consisting of \(B-1\) zeros and one sufficiently remote value make the summed score change sign at least three times; thus the requested unique root, monotone score inversion, and a uniform positive slope modulus do not follow. In addition, conditioning on the common pilot controls fluctuations about a pilot-dependent block mean, not automatically about the unconditional expectation appearing in the target. The frozen bank supplies a factorial covariance calculation but neither a pilot-fluctuation score nor a retained range that repairs these two gaps.

open_obligations.partial_result:
The established node \(lem:four\text{-}coordinate\text{-}bias\) supplies the bias
\(C_\epsilon Md/[n\log(en)]\).  The stipulated score, however, does not yet
turn this fact into the requested observable tail radius.  Indeed, for
\[
 \psi(x)=\frac12\log\frac{1+x+x^2/2}{1-x+x^2/2}
\]
one has
\[
 \psi'(x)=\frac{2(2-x^2)}{x^4+4}.
\]
Thus the score is increasing only on \((-\sqrt2,\sqrt2)\) and is decreasing
outside that interval.  More concretely, for any odd block count \(B\ge3\)
and any \(\lambda>0\), consider algebraic block outputs
\(Z_1=\cdots=Z_{B-1}=0\) and \(Z_B=R/\lambda\).  The proposed score is
\[
 S_R(t)=-(B-1)\psi(\lambda t)+\psi(R-\lambda t).
\]
For sufficiently large \(R\), continuity and
\(\psi(x)\downarrow0\) as \(x\to\infty\) give
\[
 S_R(0)>0,\quad S_R(\sqrt2/\lambda)<0,\quad
 S_R((R-\sqrt2)/\lambda)>0,\quad S_R(R/\lambda)<0.
\]
Hence the zero equation has at least three roots.  A retained-range argument
could still repair uniqueness, but no such range or a positive slope modulus
is presently part of the construction, and the unbounded outcome model does
not supply one automatically.

prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: For the stipulated symmetric score, direct differentiation gives \(\psi'(x)=2(2-x^2)/(x^4+4)\). It is increasing only for \(|x|<\sqrt2\), decreases outside that range, tends back to zero in both tails, and can produce at least three roots for an odd collection of block values. Consequently uniqueness, monotone bisection, and a uniform score-to-root error modulus are false without an additional retained-range theorem. proofs.proof_tex:
We prove the proposed statement.  Throughout, total variation is normalized to lie in \([0,1]\).

First let \(C_n\) be any interval admissible in \(\texttt{def:minimax-honest-length}\).  The exact-class point-mass priors from \(\texttt{lem:root-n-testing-priors}\), followed by \(\texttt{lem:coverage-testing-inequality}\), give
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_{d,\epsilon,M}}
 E_{Q_P^{(n)}}[|C_n|]
 \ge \kappa_\alpha M n^{-1/2},
\tag{1}
\]
where
\[
 \kappa_\alpha
 =(1-2\alpha)
 \min\!\left\{\frac14,
 \sqrt{\frac{3\log\{1+(1-2\alpha)^2\}}{32}}\right\}>0.
\]
Indeed, the target separation in that lemma is twice the displayed minimum times \(Mn^{-1/2}\), while its total-variation upper bound is \((1-2\alpha)/2\).  Taking the infimum over admissible \(C_n\) proves
\[
 \mathsf W^*_{n,d,\epsilon,M,\alpha}
 \ge \kappa_\alpha M n^{-1/2}.
\tag{2}
\]

We next prove the rare-cell bound by a confidence-interval de-Poissonization.  Put
\[
 N=4n,\qquad D=d-1.
\tag{3}
\]
Only the regime \(D\ge A\log^4N\) and \(N\ge N_0\), for constants \(A,N_0\) fixed below, needs a rare-cell construction.  In particular \(D\ge1\).  Since \(d\le c_\epsilon n\log(en)\), \(c_\epsilon\le1\), and \(N=4n\),
\[
 D\le N\log N.
\tag{4}
\]

Apply \(\texttt{lem:zeng-moment-matching-triples}\) with sample-size argument \(N\), dimension argument \(D\), and \(c_3=1\).  Choose fixed \(c_2>0\) and then \(c_1>0\) sufficiently small that
\[
 \frac{cc_1}{c_2^2}\le1,
 \qquad
 3c_2\log\!\left(\frac{3c_2}{2ec_1}\right)\ge2.
\tag{5}
\]
This is possible because the logarithm in (5) tends to infinity as \(c_1\downarrow0\).  Let \(\nu_0,\nu_1\) be the resulting distributions, orient their labels so that
\[
 h_1-h_0\ge \frac{c_4}{N\log N},
 \qquad h_j=E_{\nu_j}[p\mu],
\tag{6}
\]
and write
\[
 b=\frac{c_1\log N}{N},\qquad
 q=\frac{c_4D}{N\log N},\qquad
 \delta=4b\sqrt D.
\tag{7}
\]
Under hypothesis \(j\), draw \((p_k,\pi_k,\mu_k)\), \(1\le k\le D\), independently from \(\nu_j\).  The common first moment
\[
 a_0=E_{\nu_0}[p]=E_{\nu_1}[p]\le D^{-1}
\tag{8}
\]
allows us to append a residual coordinate
\[
 p_d=1-Da_0\ge0,\qquad \pi_d=\epsilon,\qquad \mu_d=0.
\tag{9}
\]
Define the conditioning event
\[
 E_j=
 \left\{\left|\sum_{k=1}^D p_k-Da_0\right|\le\delta,
 \ \left|\sum_{k=1}^D p_k\mu_k-Dh_j\right|\le\frac q4\right\}.
\tag{10}
\]
Independence, \(0\le p\le b\), and \(0\le p\mu\le b\) give
\[
 E_{\nu_j^{\otimes D}}
 \left[\left\{\sum_{k=1}^D(p_k-a_0)\right\}^2\right]
 =D\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_j}(p)\le Db^2
\tag{11}
\]
and
\[
 E_{\nu_j^{\otimes D}}
 \left[\left\{\sum_{k=1}^D(p_k\mu_k-h_j)\right\}^2\right]
 =D\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_j}(p\mu)\le Db^2.
\tag{12}
\]
For any centered random variable \(Z\), the pointwise inequality
\(t^2\mathbf 1\{|Z|>t\}\le Z^2\) yields
\(P(|Z|>t)\le E[Z^2]/t^2\).  Applying it to (11)--(12), then using (7), gives
\[
 P_j(E_j^c)
 \le \frac{Db^2}{\delta^2}
      +\frac{16Db^2}{q^2}
 \le \frac1{16}
      +\frac{16c_1^2\log^4N}{c_4^2D}.
\tag{13}
\]

We now derive the count-mixture distance rather than importing a squared-risk conclusion.  In one nonresidual cell, let
\[
 Z_k=(Z_{k11},Z_{k10},Z_{k0})
\tag{14}
\]
have conditionally independent coordinates with means
\[
 Np\pi\mu,\qquad Np\pi(1-\mu),\qquad Np(1-\pi),
\tag{15}
\]
respectively.  For nonnegative integers \(x,y,z\), its mixture probability under \(\nu_j\) is
\[
 E_{\nu_j}\!\left[
 e^{-Np}
 \frac{(Np\pi\mu)^x\{Np\pi(1-\mu)\}^y\{Np(1-\pi)\}^z}
 {x!y!z!}
 \right].
\tag{16}
\]
Expand \(e^{-Np}=\sum_{t\ge0}(-Np)^t/t!\).  The absolute series is summable because \(Np\le c_1\log N\).  Moreover,
\[
 p^t(p\pi\mu)^x\{p\pi(1-\mu)\}^y\{p(1-\pi)\}^z
\tag{17}
\]
is a polynomial of total degree \(t+x+y+z\) in the three coordinates
\[
 p,\qquad p\pi,\qquad p\pi\mu,
\tag{18}
\]
because \(p\pi(1-\mu)=p\pi-p\pi\mu\) and
\(p(1-\pi)=p-p\pi\).  Hence all terms of degree at most \(3K\), where \(K=c_2\log N\), cancel between the two mixture probabilities by the moment identities in \(\texttt{lem:zeng-moment-matching-triples}\).

For either prior, the sum of the absolute remaining terms over all \(x,y,z,t\) with \(x+y+z+t>3K\) is at most
\[
 \sum_{r>3K}\frac{(2c_1\log N)^r}{r!}
 =N^{2c_1}P\{W>3K\},
 \qquad W\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(2c_1\log N).
\tag{19}
\]
To verify the tail bound used in (19), if \(W\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\) and \(L>e\lambda\), exponential Markov with \(t=\log(L/\lambda)>1\) gives
\[
 P(W>L)
 \le \exp\{\lambda(e^t-1)-tL\}
 =e^{-\lambda}\left(\frac{e\lambda}{L}\right)^L.
\tag{20}
\]
Taking \(\lambda=2c_1\log N\), \(L=3c_2\log N\), and using (5), equations (19)--(20) give
\[
 \sum_{r>3K}\frac{(2c_1\log N)^r}{r!}
 \le
 \left(\frac{2ec_1}{3c_2}\right)^{3c_2\log N}
 \le N^{-2}.
\tag{21}
\]
The total-variation distance is one half the \(\ell^1\) distance of the mixture mass functions.  Equations (16)--(21), applied to both priors, therefore imply
\[
 \|\mathcal L_0(Z_k)-\mathcal L_1(Z_k)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le N^{-2}.
\tag{22}
\]
The \(D\) triples in (14) are independent before conditioning, and the residual-cell count has the same law under both hypotheses.  A telescoping expansion of the two product mass functions, followed by the triangle inequality, thus yields
\[
 \|\mathcal L_0(Z)-\mathcal L_1(Z)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le \sum_{k=1}^D
 \|\mathcal L_0(Z_k)-\mathcal L_1(Z_k)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le \frac{D}{N^2}
 \le \frac{\log N}{N},
\tag{23}
\]
where the last step uses (4).

Conditioning a probability measure \(\Gamma\) on an event \(E\) changes it in total variation by exactly \(\Gamma(E^c)\); applying a common observation kernel cannot increase total variation.  Consequently (13) and (23) imply that the two predictive count laws \(\widetilde Q_0,\widetilde Q_1\), after conditioning their parameter priors on \(E_0,E_1\), satisfy
\[
 \|\widetilde Q_0-\widetilde Q_1\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le \frac18
 +\frac{32c_1^2\log^4N}{c_4^2D}
 +\frac{\log N}{N}.
\tag{24}
\]
Choose \(A\) and then \(N_0\) large enough that, whenever
\(D\ge A\log^4N\) and \(N\ge N_0\), the last two terms in (24) are at most \(1/8\).  Then
\[
 \|\widetilde Q_0-\widetilde Q_1\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\frac14.
\tag{25}
\]

The relaxed one-arm targets are
\[
 \vartheta=M\sum_{k=1}^D p_k\mu_k.
\tag{26}
\]
Under the prior conditioned on \(E_j\), they lie in
\[
 \widetilde{\mathcal T}_j
 =\left[M\left(Dh_j-\frac q4\right),
         M\left(Dh_j+\frac q4\right)\right].
\tag{27}
\]
Equations (6)--(7) give the direct separation
\[
 \Delta(\widetilde{\mathcal T}_0,\widetilde{\mathcal T}_1)
 \ge M\{D(h_1-h_0)-q/2\}
 \ge \frac{Mq}{2}.
\tag{28}
\]
Also, after (9), the total unnormalized mass \(S\) obeys on \(E_j\)
\[
 S=p_d+\sum_{k=1}^D p_k,
 \qquad |S-1|\le\delta.
\tag{29}
\]
Increasing \(N_0\) if necessary, (4) and (7) ensure
\[
 \delta\le4c_1\frac{\log^{3/2}N}{\sqrt N}\le\frac13.
\tag{30}
\]

It remains to connect this relaxed experiment to the exact class defining \(\mathsf W^*_{n,d,\epsilon,M,\alpha}\).  Fix a parameter vector in either conditioned prior and normalize its cell masses to
\[
 p_k^\circ=p_k/S,\qquad 1\le k\le d.
\tag{31}
\]
Construct a full-data law \(P^\circ\) as follows: given \(X=k\), draw
\(A\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_k)\), set \(Y(0)=0\), draw
\(Y(1)=M B_k\) with \(B_k\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\mu_k)\) independently of \(A\) conditional on \(X\), and set \(Y=Y(A)\).  Consistency and conditional exchangeability hold by construction.  The cited support gives fixed overlap.  Furthermore,
\[
 |E[Y\mid A=1,X=k]|=M\mu_k\le M,
 \qquad E[Y\mid A=0,X=k]=0,
\tag{32}
\]
and, for the treated arm,
\[
 E[(Y-M\mu_k)^4\mid A=1,X=k]
 =M^4E[(B_k-\mu_k)^4]
 \le M^4,
\tag{33}
\]
while the control-arm central fourth moment is zero.  Thus (31)--(33) and
\(\texttt{def:global-law-class}\) show
\[
 P^\circ\in\mathcal P_{d,\epsilon,M}.
\tag{34}
\]
By \(\texttt{def:ate-functional}\),
\[
 \tau(P^\circ)=\frac{M\sum_{k=1}^Dp_k\mu_k}{S}
 =\frac{\vartheta}{S}.
\tag{35}
\]
Since \(0\le\sum p_k\mu_k\le S\), equations (29) and (35) yield
\[
 |\tau(P^\circ)-\vartheta|
 =M\left(\sum_{k=1}^Dp_k\mu_k\right)
   \frac{|1-S|}{S}
 \le M|1-S|le M\delta.
\tag{36}
\]

Under the Poisson experiment, let \(R\) be the total count over all cells and all three observable labels.  Conditional on the parameter,
\[
 R\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(NS),
\tag{37}
\]
and, conditional on \(R=r\), a parameter-free uniform ordering of the \(r\) observed labels is an iid sample from the observed margin of \(P^\circ\).  Attach such an ordering to the count statistic; because this is a common Markov kernel, (25) remains valid for the augmented experiment.

Let
\[
 L(C_n)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_{d,\epsilon,M}}
 E_{Q_P^{(n)}}[|C_n|].
\tag{38}
\]
Define an interval in the augmented Poisson experiment by
\[
 \widetilde C=
 \begin{cases}
 C_n(O_1^*,\ldots,O_n^*)+[-M\delta,M\delta],&R\ge n,\\
 [-2M,2M],&R<n,
 \end{cases}
\tag{39}
\]
where \(O_1^*,\ldots,O_n^*\) are the first \(n\) observations in the attached uniform ordering and \(+\) is Minkowski addition.  Conditional on every \(R=r\ge n\), these \(n\) observations have law \(Q_{P^\circ}^{(n)}\).  Hence admissibility of \(C_n\), (34), and (36) show pointwise for every relaxed parameter satisfying (29) that
\[
 P\{\vartheta\in\widetilde C\mid R=r\}\ge1-\alpha,
 \qquad r\ge n.
\tag{40}
\]
When \(R<n\), equations (26), (29), and (30) give
\(0\le\vartheta\le M(1+\delta)<2M\), so the second branch of (39) covers surely.  Thus
\[
 P\{\vartheta\in\widetilde C\}\ge1-\alpha
\tag{41}
\]
for every parameter in either conditioned relaxed prior.

The lower tail in (37) is exponentially small.  Indeed, with
\(\lambda=NS\ge(2/3)N=8n/3\), one has \(n\le\lambda/2\); exponential Markov at \(t=\log2\) gives
\[
 P\{\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\le\lambda/2\}
 \le \exp\{\lambda((\log2)/2-1/2)\}
 \le e^{-\lambda/8}\le e^{-n/3}.
\tag{42}
\]
For every \(r\ge n\), (34), (38), and the conditional iid property imply that the conditional expected length of the first interval in (39), before enlargement, is at most \(L(C_n)\).  Therefore
\[
 E[|\widetilde C|]
 \le L(C_n)+2M\delta+4Me^{-n/3}
\tag{43}
\]
under either conditioned prior-predictive law.

For completeness, we apply coverage to length directly in this augmented experiment.  Let
\(G_j=\{\widetilde C\cap\widetilde{\mathcal T}_j\ne\varnothing\}\).  Equation (41) and prior support on (27) give
\[
 \widetilde Q_j(G_j)\ge1-\alpha.
\tag{44}
\]
By (25),
\[
 \widetilde Q_0(G_1)
 \ge\widetilde Q_1(G_1)
   -\|\widetilde Q_0-\widetilde Q_1\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \ge1-\alpha-\frac14.
\tag{45}
\]
The union bound, (44), and (45) yield
\[
 \widetilde Q_0(G_0\cap G_1)
 \ge1-2\alpha-\frac14>\frac14,
\tag{46}
\]
where the last inequality uses \(\alpha<1/4\).  On \(G_0\cap G_1\), the interval has length at least the separation in (28).  Thus
\[
 E_{\widetilde Q_0}[|\widetilde C|]
 \ge \frac{Mq}{2}\left(1-2\alpha-\frac14\right)
 \ge\frac{Mq}{8}.
\tag{47}
\]
Combining (43) and (47) gives
\[
 L(C_n)\ge\frac{Mq}{8}-2M\delta-4Me^{-n/3}.
\tag{48}
\]

Finally choose \(A\) still larger, if necessary, so that
\[
 D\ge A\log^4N
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \frac{2\delta}{q}
 =\frac{8c_1\log^2N}{c_4\sqrt D}\le\frac1{32},
\tag{49}
\]
and increase \(N_0\) so that \(4e^{-n/3}\le q/32\) throughout this regime.  The latter is possible because (7) and \(D\ge A\log^4N\) imply
\(q\ge c_4A\log^3N/N\), whereas \(N=4n\).  Equations (48)--(49) then prove
\[
 L(C_n)\ge\frac{Mq}{16}
 \ge c_\epsilon M\frac{d}{n\log(en)}.
\tag{50}
\]
For the second inequality, use \(D=d-1\ge d/2\) in the present regime,
\(N=4n\), and \(\log N\le(\log4)\log(en)\).

It remains only to check the complementary ranges.  If \(N<N_0\), then
\(d/[n\log(en)]\le1\le C_{N_0}n^{-1/2}\).  If
\(D<A\log^4N\), then
\[
 \frac{d}{n\log(en)}
 \le C_A\frac{1+\log^3(en)}{n}
 \le C_A' n^{-1/2}.
\tag{51}
\]
The last inequality is uniform because
\(\log(en)=1+\log n\le(1+6/e)n^{1/6}\), the latter following by maximizing
\((\log x)x^{-1/6}\) over \(x\ge1\).  Thus (2) also dominates the rare-cell term in every range not covered by (50).

Equations (2), (50), and (51) show, for all
\(d\le c_\epsilon n\log(en)\),
\[
 \mathsf W^*_{n,d,\epsilon,M,\alpha}
 \ge c_{\epsilon,\alpha}M
 \max\!\left\{n^{-1/2},\frac{d}{n\log(en)}\right\}
 \ge \frac{c_{\epsilon,\alpha}M}{2}
 \min\!\left\{1,n^{-1/2}+\frac{d}{n\log(en)}\right\}.
\tag{52}
\]
The final expression is a constant multiple of \(r_{n,d,M}\) by
\(\texttt{def:frontier-scale}\), which proves the claim.

added_lemmas.statement:
There exist constants \(c,c'>0\) such that, for any \(c_1,c_2,c_3>0\) satisfying \(cc_1c_3/c_2^2\le 1\) and \(d\le c_3n\log n\), there are two probability distributions \(\nu_0,\nu_1\) on triples \((p,\pi,\mu)\) with the following properties.  Almost surely under either distribution,
\[
 0\le p\le \frac{c_1\log n}{n},\qquad
 \epsilon\le\pi\le1-\epsilon,\qquad 0\le\mu\le1.
\]
Writing \(K=c_2\log n\), for all nonnegative integers \(i,j,k\) with \(i+j+k\le3K\),
\[
 E_{\nu_0}\!\left[p^i(p\pi)^j(p\pi\mu)^k\right]
 =E_{\nu_1}\!\left[p^i(p\pi)^j(p\pi\mu)^k\right].
\]
Moreover,
\[
 a_0:=E_{\nu_0}[p]=E_{\nu_1}[p]\le\frac1d,
 \qquad
 \left|E_{\nu_0}[p\mu]-E_{\nu_1}[p\mu]\right|
 \ge \frac{c_4}{n\log n},
 \qquad c_4=\frac{cc'c_1}{c_2^2}.
\]

proofs.proof_tex:
Write
\[
 p_{k,n}=P_n(X=k),\qquad
 \pi_{k,n}=P_n(A=1\mid X=k),\qquad
 \sigma_{ak,n}^2=E_{P_n}\!\left[(Y-\mu_{ak,n})^2\mid X=k,A=a\right],
\]
where the conditional quantities are defined because the assumed lower bound
\(p_{k,n}\ge c_0/d>0\) gives every cell positive mass.  The conditional
fourth-moment assumption and the elementary inequality
\((E|Z|^2)^2\le E|Z|^4\), obtained by expanding
\(E[(Z^2-EZ^2)^2]\ge0\), give
\[
 \sigma_{ak,n}^2\le M^2.                                             \tag{1}
\]
Put
\[
 h_{k,n}=\mu_{1k,n}-\mu_{0k,n}-\tau(P_n),\qquad
 V_n=V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n),\qquad \phi_n=\phi_{P_n}.
\]
By the identifying functional, \(\sum_kp_{k,n}h_{k,n}=0\).  Conditional on
\(X=k\), each outcome residual in the efficient influence function has mean
zero.  Its treated and control summands have product zero because
\(A(1-A)=0\).  Expanding the square in the definition of \(V_n\) therefore
gives the orthogonal decomposition
\[
 V_n=
 \sum_{k=1}^d p_{k,n}\left\{
 h_{k,n}^2+\frac{\sigma_{1k,n}^2}{\pi_{k,n}}
              +\frac{\sigma_{0k,n}^2}{1-\pi_{k,n}}
 \right\}.                                                           \tag{2}
\]
All three summands in braces are nonnegative.  Fixed overlap consequently
implies, for \(a\in\{0,1\}\),
\[
 \sum_{k=1}^d p_{k,n}\sigma_{ak,n}^2\le V_n,
 \qquad
 \sum_{k=1}^d p_{k,n}h_{k,n}^2\le V_n.                               \tag{3}
\]

We next analyze the explicit saturated one-step estimator.  For validation
fold \(I_s\), let \(m_{s,n}=n-|I_s|\), let
\(\mathcal D_n^{(-s)}=(O_j:j\notin I_s)\), and define
\[
 q_{1k,n}=p_{k,n}\pi_{k,n},\qquad
 q_{0k,n}=p_{k,n}(1-\pi_{k,n}).
\]
Balance and overlap give
\[
 q_{ak,n}\ge q_*:=\frac{c_0\epsilon}{d}>0.                            \tag{4}
\]
Since \(K_0\) is fixed and the fold sizes differ by at most one, there is a
constant \(c_K>0\) such that \(m_{s,n}\ge c_Kn\) for every \(s\) and all
large \(n\).  If \(N\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,q)\), then
\[
 P(N=0)=(1-q)^m\le e^{-mq}.                                           \tag{5}
\]
Moreover, when \(mq\ge1\), splitting according to \(N\ge mq/2\) and using
\(P(|N-mq|\ge mq/2)\le4\operatorname{Var}(N)/(m^2q^2)\le4/(mq)\), which
follows by applying Markov's inequality to \((N-mq)^2\), yields
\[
 E\!\left[\frac{\mathbf1\{N>0\}}{N}\right]
 \le \frac{2}{mq}+P(0<N<mq/2)\le\frac{6}{mq}.                         \tag{6}
\]

Let
\[
 e_{ak}^{(-s)}=\widehat\mu_{ak}^{(-s)}-\mu_{ak,n},\qquad
 \delta_k^{(-s)}=\widehat\pi_k^{(-s)}-\pi_{k,n}.
\]
Conditional on a nonzero training arm-cell count, the corresponding outcome
mean is unbiased and has conditional variance
\(\sigma_{ak,n}^2/N_{ak}^{(-s)}\).  On an empty arm-cell its zero fallback
has squared error at most \(M^2\) by the cell-mean envelope.  Equations
\((4)\)--\((6)\) thus imply, uniformly over the fixed set of \((a,k,s)\),
\[
 E[(e_{ak}^{(-s)})^2]
 \le \frac{C\sigma_{ak,n}^2}{n}+CM^2e^{-cn}.                          \tag{7}
\]
For the propensity estimate, condition on the number of training observations
with \(X=k\).  On a nonempty cell the empirical treatment fraction is
unbiased with conditional variance at most the reciprocal of that count; on
an empty cell its squared error is at most one.  Clipping cannot increase its
distance from \(\pi_{k,n}\in[\epsilon,1-\epsilon]\).  Applying
\((5)\)--\((6)\) with the cell mass \(p_{k,n}\ge c_0/d\) gives
\[
 E[(\delta_k^{(-s)})^2]\le \frac Cn+Ce^{-cn}.                         \tag{8}
\]
Here and below \(c,C>0\) may depend on
\((d,c_0,\epsilon,K_0)\), but not on \(n\) or on the particular row law.

Define the oracle uncentered score
\[
 \psi_n(O)=\mu_{1X,n}-\mu_{0X,n}
 +\frac{A(Y-\mu_{1X,n})}{\pi_{X,n}}
 -\frac{(1-A)(Y-\mu_{0X,n})}{1-\pi_{X,n}}
 =\tau(P_n)+\phi_n(O).                                                \tag{9}
\]
For \(i\in I_s\), put \(D_{i,s}=\widehat\psi_i-\psi_n(O_i)\).
Independence of the validation observation and its training sample follows
from i.i.d. sampling and deterministic sample splitting.  Direct substitution
in the score, followed by conditional expectation over the validation
observation, gives
\[
 E[D_{i,s}\mid X_i=k,\mathcal D_n^{(-s)}]
 =\delta_k^{(-s)}\left\{
 \frac{e_{1k}^{(-s)}}{\widehat\pi_k^{(-s)}}
 +\frac{e_{0k}^{(-s)}}{1-\widehat\pi_k^{(-s)}}
 \right\}.                                                          \tag{10}
\]
The two denominators in \((10)\) are at least \(\epsilon/2\).  If
\(B_{s,n}=E[D_{i,s}\mid\mathcal D_n^{(-s)}]\), the inequality
\(E|UV|\le(EU^2EV^2)^{1/2}\), obtained from
\(E[(U-tV)^2]\ge0\) and optimization over \(t\), together with
\((3)\), \((7)\), and \((8)\), gives
\[
 E|B_{s,n}|
 \le C\left\{\frac{\sqrt{V_n}}{n}+Me^{-cn}\right\}.                \tag{11}
\]
The mean envelope gives \(|h_{k,n}|\le4M\).  The inequality
\((x_1+x_2+x_3)^4\le27(x_1^4+x_2^4+x_3^4)\), the conditional fourth-moment
bound, and overlap therefore give
\[
 E_{P_n}[\phi_n(O)^4]\le C_\epsilon M^4,
 \qquad V_n\le C_\epsilon M^2.                                      \tag{12}
\]
It follows from \((11)\)--\((12)\) and Markov's inequality that
\(\sqrt n B_{s,n}=o_{Q_{P_n}^{(n)}}(1)\), uniformly over the fixed number
of folds.

Before taking conditional expectations in \((10)\), the same substitution
in the score and the inequality \((x_1+\cdots+x_r)^2\le r\sum_jx_j^2\)
show that
\[
 E[D_{i,s}^2\mid\mathcal D_n^{(-s)}]
 \le C\sum_{k=1}^d p_{k,n}\left[
 (e_{1k}^{(-s)})^2+(e_{0k}^{(-s)})^2
 +(\delta_k^{(-s)})^2
       (\sigma_{1k,n}^2+\sigma_{0k,n}^2)
 \right].                                                           \tag{13}
\]
The residual multipliers in this calculation are bounded by a constant
depending only on \(\epsilon\), because both the true and clipped estimated
propensities are bounded away from zero and one.  Taking expectations in
\((13)\) and applying \((3)\), \((7)\), and \((8)\) yields
\[
 E[D_{i,s}^2]\le \frac{CV_n}{n}+CM^2e^{-cn}=o(M^2).                  \tag{14}
\]
Conditional on each training sample, the centered variables
\(D_{i,s}-B_{s,n}\), \(i\in I_s\), are independent.  Applying Markov's
inequality to their conditional squared sum, then using \((11)\), \((14)\),
and the fact that there are only \(K_0\) folds, proves
\[
 \frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{s=0}^{K_0-1}\sum_{i\in I_s}D_{i,s}
 =o_{Q_{P_n}^{(n)}}(1).                                               \tag{15}
\]
Combining \((9)\) and \((15)\) gives
\[
 \sqrt n\{\widehat\tau^{\mathrm{OS}}-\tau(P_n)\}
 =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_n(O_i)
  +o_{Q_{P_n}^{(n)}}(1).                                              \tag{16}
\]
The leading sum has mean zero and variance \(V_n\) by \((2)\).  Markov's
inequality applied to its square and the premise \(V_n/M^2\to0\) therefore
imply
\[
 \sqrt n\{\widehat\tau^{\mathrm{OS}}-\tau(P_n)\}
 \longrightarrow0                                                    \tag{17}
\]
in \(Q_{P_n}^{(n)}\)-probability.

For the variance estimator, \((12)\) gives
\[
 E\!\left[\left\{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_n(O_i)^2-V_n\right\}^2\right]
 \le \frac{C_\epsilon M^4}{n}.                                      \tag{18}
\]
Also, averaging \((14)\) over observations and using Markov's inequality
gives
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nD_{i,s(i)}^2=o_{Q_{P_n}^{(n)}}(M^2),             \tag{19}
\]
where \(s(i)\) is the fold containing \(i\).  Because centering at the
sample mean minimizes an empirical sum of squares,
\[
 0\le\widehat V^{\mathrm{OS}}
 \le\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\{\widehat\psi_i-\tau(P_n)\}^2
 \le\frac2n\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_n(O_i)^2
     +\frac2n\sum_{i=1}^nD_{i,s(i)}^2.                               \tag{20}
\]
Equations \((18)\)--\((20)\) and \(V_n/M^2\to0\) prove
\[
 \widehat V^{\mathrm{OS}}/M^2\longrightarrow0                       \tag{21}
\]
in probability.

It remains to transfer these conclusions to the corrected heavy--light
outputs.  Let
\[
 \mathcal H_n=
 \left\{\min_{a\in\{0,1\},\,1\le k\le d}N_{ak}^{(0)}
             >256\log(en)\right\}.
\]
For each pilot arm-cell, \(N_{ak}^{(0)}\) is binomial with mean
\(\nu_{ak,n}=|I_0|q_{ak,n}\ge c_Kq_*n\).  For all sufficiently large
\(n\), \(256\log(en)\le\nu_{ak,n}/2\).  If
\(N\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,q)\), exponential Markov with
\(t=\log2\) gives directly
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 P(N\le mq/2)
 &\le e^{tmq/2}E[e^{-tN}]\\
 &=e^{tmq/2}(1-q+qe^{-t})^m\\
 &\le\exp\{mq[t/2-(1-e^{-t})]\}
 \le e^{-mq/8},
 \end{aligned}                                                       \tag{22}
\]
because \(1-u\le e^{-u}\) and
\((1-\log2)/2>1/8\).  A union bound over the fixed \(2d\) pilot arm-cells
therefore yields the advertised, slightly looser bound
\[
 Q_{P_n}^{(n)}(\mathcal H_n^c)
 \le2dK_0\exp(-c_Kq_*n/8)=o(1).                                      \tag{23}
\]
The corrected all-heavy clause in the heavy--light construction is an exact
sample identity:
\[
 (\widehat\tau^{\mathrm{HL}},\widehat V^{\mathrm{HL}})
 =(\widehat\tau^{\mathrm{OS}},\widehat V^{\mathrm{OS}})
 \quad\text{on }\mathcal H_n.                                        \tag{24}
\]
Thus, for every \(r>0\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 Q_{P_n}^{(n)}\!\left(\sqrt n
   |\widehat\tau^{\mathrm{HL}}-\tau(P_n)|>r\right)
 &\le Q_{P_n}^{(n)}(\mathcal H_n^c)
  +Q_{P_n}^{(n)}\!\left(\sqrt n
   |\widehat\tau^{\mathrm{OS}}-\tau(P_n)|>r\right),\\
 Q_{P_n}^{(n)}\!\left(\widehat V^{\mathrm{HL}}/M^2>r\right)
 &\le Q_{P_n}^{(n)}(\mathcal H_n^c)
  +Q_{P_n}^{(n)}\!\left(\widehat V^{\mathrm{OS}}/M^2>r\right).
 \end{aligned}                                                       \tag{25}
\]
Equations \((17)\), \((21)\), and \((23)\) prove both heavy--light
conclusions.

Finally, the non-implication is witnessed inside the same class.  Let
\(P_n=P^0\) for every \(n\), where \(X\) is uniform on
\(\{1,\ldots,d\}\), \(A\) is independent of \(X\) with
\(P^0(A=1)=1/2\), and \(Y(0)=Y(1)=Y=0\) almost surely.  Consistency and
conditional exchangeability hold by construction.  Fixed overlap holds
because \(\epsilon<1/2\); the cell-mean and conditional fourth-moment bounds
hold with value zero; and \(p_k=1/d\ge c_0/d\).  The efficient influence
function is identically zero, so
\[
 V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P^0)=0.                                            \tag{26}
\]
Consequently a statistic divided by \(\sqrt{V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P^0)}\), a
variance ratio with denominator \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P^0)\), and a Wald
endpoint comparison normalized by
\(\sqrt{V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P^0)/n}\) are all undefined.  Thus none of these
studentized or relative conclusions is a consequence of the proposition's
premises on the entire stated class.  This witness does not claim failure of
an absolute \(o_P(n^{-1/2})\) endpoint comparison, which is why the corrected
statement restricts its final clause to studentized or relative Wald
equivalence.

Let \(\mathbf P=(P_n)\) satisfy \(P_n\in\mathcal P_{d,\epsilon,M}\),
\(d_n=d\) fixed, \(P_n(X=k)\ge c_0/d\) for every \(k\), and
\(V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n)/M^2\to0\).  Then
\(\sqrt n\{\widehat\tau^{\mathrm{HL}}-\tau(P_n)\}\to0\) and
\(\sqrt n\{\widehat\tau^{\mathrm{OS}}-\tau(P_n)\}\to0\) in
\(Q_{P_n}^{(n)}\)-probability, while
\(\widehat V^{\mathrm{HL}}/M^2\to0\) and
\(\widehat V^{\mathrm{OS}}/M^2\to0\).  No conclusion that requires division
by \(\sqrt{V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n)}\) follows from these conditions alone; in
particular, they imply neither a standardized normal limit, nor ratio
consistency of either variance estimator, nor endpoint equivalence after
normalization by \(\sqrt{V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_n)/n}\).
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The zero-variance law makes studentized and relative Wald quantities undefined, but it does not refute an absolute endpoint difference of order \(o_P(n^{-1/2})\).  The final clause is therefore narrowed exactly to the relative or studentized claim supported by the witness.
